The_Earth_System_Chapter_3.2: Figures 3-1 and 3-2: Venus, Earth, and Mars are shown approximately to scale. The wave diagram marks wavelength as the distance between successive crests; a dashed curve shows the same wave a short time later, moving right at speed c. The relation is wavelength times frequency = c.
The_Earth_System_Chapter_3.3: Figure 3-3: The electromagnetic spectrum is arranged by increasing wavelength, from gamma/X-rays through ultraviolet, visible, infrared, and microwave/radio radiation. The expanded visible band runs from violet near 0.4 micrometers to red near 0.7 micrometers. Shorter wavelength corresponds to higher frequency and photon energy.
The_Earth_System_Chapter_3.4: Figure 3-4: Parallel light rays strike a sheet first perpendicular to the beam and then at an angle. Tilting the sheet spreads the intercepted radiation over a larger surface area, reducing the incoming energy per unit area.
The_Earth_System_Chapter_3.5: Figure 3-5: Concentric orbits around a central light source illustrate the inverse-square law, S = S0(r0/r)^2. At twice the original distance the same radiation is spread over four times the area, so the flux is one quarter as large.
The_Earth_System_Chapter_3.6: Table 3-1 compares water's freezing/boiling points: 32/212 degrees F, 0/100 degrees C, and 273.15/373.15 K. Figure 3-6 shows a cast-iron ball at room temperature and at progressively higher temperatures: the emitted radiation grows stronger and moves into visible wavelengths as it is heated.
The_Earth_System_Chapter_3.7: Figures 3-7 and 3-8: A blackbody spectrum plots radiation flux against wavelength. Its peak obeys Wien's law, lambda_max = 2898/T (micrometers for T in kelvins), while the area under the curve gives total flux proportional to T^4. The Sun's much hotter spectrum peaks near 0.5 micrometers; Earth's spectrum peaks near 10 micrometers in the infrared. The Sun emits more per unit surface area at every wavelength shown.
The_Earth_System_Chapter_3.9: Box Figure 3-1: Earth intercepts sunlight over a disk of area pi R^2 but emits infrared over its entire spherical area, 4 pi R^2. Some incident sunlight is reflected. Equating absorbed and emitted energy gives sigma Te^4 = (S/4)(1-A), where A is planetary albedo. The factor of four comes from the disk-to-sphere area ratio.
The_Earth_System_Chapter_3.10: Box Figure 3-2: The idealized one-layer atmosphere passes solar radiation but absorbs surface infrared. It emits infrared both upward to space and downward to the surface. The arrows distinguish incoming S/4, reflected (S/4)A, absorbed (S/4)(1-A), surface emission sigma Ts^4, and atmospheric emission sigma Ta^4 in each direction. In this idealized model Ts = 2^(1/4) Te; it overestimates the actual greenhouse warming because real atmospheric absorption is incomplete.
The_Earth_System_Chapter_3.11: Tables 3-2 and 3-3 distinguish abundant atmospheric gases from greenhouse gases. Nitrogen, oxygen, and argon dominate atmospheric composition, whereas water vapor, carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, ozone, and the listed CFCs absorb infrared. Concentrations are values reported by this edition, not current measurements; the CO2 abundance in Table 3-2 is explicitly dated 2002.
The_Earth_System_Chapter_3.12: Figure 3-9: Pressure falls strongly with altitude (the pressure axis is logarithmic). The temperature profile decreases through the troposphere, increases through the stratosphere, decreases through the mesosphere, and increases again in the thermosphere. Figure 3-10 uses a heated pot to distinguish radiation from the burner, conduction through the pot/handle, convection within the water, and latent heat carried away by evaporating water.
The_Earth_System_Chapter_3.13: Figure 3-11: Ozone concentration is plotted against altitude. It is small near the surface, reaches a broad maximum in the stratosphere around 30-35 km, and decreases above that level. This profile is distinct from the altitude at which solar heating is greatest.
The_Earth_System_Chapter_3.14: Figure 3-12: An incoming infrared photon is absorbed by a water molecule, changing it from a slower to a faster rotational state. The before/after molecular drawing connects absorption to molecular motion.
The_Earth_System_Chapter_3.15: Figure 3-13 plots atmospheric absorption percentage against wavelength. Absorption varies by band: H2O, CO2, and O3 absorb strongly at characteristic wavelengths, while an atmospheric window occurs roughly between 8 and 12 micrometers, interrupted by ozone absorption near 9.6 micrometers. CO2 has a strong band near 15 micrometers. Figures 3-14 and 3-15 compare bending of a three-atom CO2 molecule with rotation/vibration of symmetric two-atom molecules; the symmetry difference helps explain why N2 and O2 are poor infrared absorbers.
The_Earth_System_Chapter_3.16: Figures 3-16 and 3-17 contrast an extensive cloud-covered view of Earth with low layered stratus and high wispy cirrus. The cloud examples support the distinction between strong reflection by low, thick clouds and the infrared effects of high, thin clouds.
The_Earth_System_Chapter_3.17: Figure 3-18 places low thick and high thin clouds on an altitude-temperature profile. The higher clouds are colder and radiate less infrared to space, which can enhance warming. Figure 3-19 is the global energy budget normalized to 100 units of incoming solar energy: 30 are reflected (25 by the atmosphere and 5 by the surface), 25 are absorbed by the atmosphere, and 45 by the surface. The surface also receives 88 units of downward atmospheric infrared and loses 104 by radiation, 24 by evaporation, and 5 by thermals. Outgoing infrared at the top of the atmosphere is 70; internal exchanges can exceed the external input because energy is absorbed and re-emitted repeatedly.
The_Earth_System_Chapter_3.19: Figures 3-20 and 3-21 show positive feedback loops. Warmer surface -> more atmospheric water vapor -> stronger greenhouse effect -> further warming. Warmer surface -> less snow/ice -> lower planetary albedo -> more absorbed sunlight -> further warming. Cooling reverses each chain while still reinforcing the initial change.
The_Earth_System_Chapter_3.20: Figure 3-22 shows the stabilizing negative feedback between surface temperature and outgoing infrared: warming increases infrared energy loss, which opposes the warming. This damping acts alongside the positive water-vapor and ice-albedo feedbacks.

The_Earth_System_Chapter_5.2: Figure 5-1 combines trade winds and westerlies with surface currents. Their action produces subtropical ocean gyres, clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and counterclockwise in the Southern Hemisphere.
The_Earth_System_Chapter_5.3: Figure 5-2 maps the major warm and cool surface currents, including the Gulf Stream, North Atlantic Drift, Kuroshio, California, Canary, Peru/Humboldt, Benguela, and Antarctic circumpolar flow. Warm currents generally carry tropical water poleward along western basin boundaries; cooler return currents flow equatorward along eastern boundaries.
The_Earth_System_Chapter_5.4: Figure 5-3(a) shows an Ekman spiral: current speed decreases and direction turns with depth. The net transport is 90 degrees to the wind (right in the Northern Hemisphere). Panel (b) shows Ekman transport from the trade-wind and westerly sides converging toward a subtropical gyre's center.
The_Earth_System_Chapter_5.5: Figure 5-4 contrasts convergence, which raises the sea surface and pushes water downward, with divergence, which lowers the surface and draws deeper water upward. Figure 5-5 shows how the elevated gyre center creates an outward pressure-gradient force balanced by Coriolis deflection; the resulting geostrophic current circulates around the mound rather than flowing directly downhill.
The_Earth_System_Chapter_5.7: Figure 5-6 sketches equatorial east-west atmospheric overturning, with rising rainy air over warm regions and subsidence elsewhere. Figure 5-7 compares the tropical Pacific ocean in normal conditions and an El Nino event: easterly trade winds normally pile warm water in the west and permit eastern upwelling; weakened/reversed winds allow warm water to spread east and suppress the usual cold-water upwelling.
The_Earth_System_Chapter_5.8: Figure 5-8 is a positive ocean-atmosphere feedback linking western-Pacific sea-surface warmth, convection, easterly surface winds, and westward ocean currents. Figure 5-9 maps warm sea-surface-temperature anomalies across the central/eastern equatorial Pacific during the 1997-98 El Nino event.
The_Earth_System_Chapter_5.9: Figure 5-10 shows the eastward displacement of tropical Pacific convection during an ENSO event. Figure 5-11 plots Tahiti and Darwin pressure anomalies and their Southern Oscillation Index through time; the two pressure records often vary oppositely, and strongly negative SOI values identify warm El Nino episodes such as 1982-83 and 1997-98.
The_Earth_System_Chapter_5.12: Figure 5-12 maps typical December-February ENSO temperature/rainfall anomalies, with wet/warm central-Pacific conditions and dryness around parts of Indonesia and Australia. These are broad composite patterns, not predictions for every event. Table 5-1 shows that chloride and sodium make up the largest shares of dissolved ocean salts.
The_Earth_System_Chapter_5.14: Figure 5-13 compares vertical temperature, salinity, and density profiles. A relatively uniform surface mixed layer overlies a transition zone: temperature decreases rapidly through the thermocline, salinity changes through the halocline, and density increases through the pycnocline. The deep ocean changes more slowly with depth.
The_Earth_System_Chapter_5.15: Figures 5-14 and 5-15 compare Atlantic and Pacific latitude-depth sections. Warm water is mainly shallow at low latitudes; cold water extends upward at high latitudes. Salinity sections show distinct water masses and an Atlantic Mediterranean-outflow feature, illustrating that salinity structure need not mirror temperature structure.
The_Earth_System_Chapter_5.16: Figure 5-16 locates the Weddell Sea and circulation around Antarctica. Sea-ice production rejects salt into the water below, creating very cold, saline, dense water that sinks and contributes to Antarctic Bottom Water. Arrows connect this source with circumpolar circulation and incoming North Atlantic deep water.
The_Earth_System_Chapter_5.17: Figure 5-17 maps spreading routes of North Atlantic Deep Water and Antarctic Bottom Water through connected basins. Figure 5-18 maps near-bottom radiocarbon differences: stronger radiocarbon depletion generally marks longer isolation from atmospheric exchange, tracing progressively older deep water away from formation regions. Mixing prevents the values from being a simple literal clock for every water parcel.
The_Earth_System_Chapter_5.19: Box Figure 5-4 plots exponential radioactive decay. After one, two, and three half-lives, the parent isotope remaining is 50%, 25%, and 12.5%; the daughter product grows correspondingly. The generic diagram's illustrative half-life is separate from carbon-14's stated half-life of 5,730 years.
The_Earth_System_Chapter_5.20: Figure 5-19 is an idealized global conveyor: solid arrows show cold salty deep currents, dashed arrows warm shallow return currents, and a North Atlantic label marks ocean-to-air heat transfer. Figure 5-20 maps ocean-color-derived productivity. Higher values occur near many coasts and upwelling zones, while central subtropical gyres are relatively unproductive because surface nutrients are depleted.
The_Earth_System_Chapter_5.21: Figure 5-21 maps temperature and salinity at 1,000 m in the North Atlantic. A relatively warm, saline tongue spreads westward from the Mediterranean outflow, illustrating how a water mass can be traced below the surface.
The_Earth_System_Chapter_5.22: Figure 5-22 plots Northern Hemisphere poleward heat transport against latitude, separating the atmosphere, ocean, and their total. Ocean transport is especially important at low latitudes; the atmosphere dominates farther poleward. The total peaks in the subtropics/midlatitudes and falls toward the pole.

The_Earth_System_Chapter_4.3: The boxed ideal-gas explanation links pressure, volume, and temperature: at fixed temperature P_initial V_initial = P_final V_final; at fixed pressure V_initial/T_initial = V_final/T_final. The combined equation is PV = mRT, with temperature in kelvins and R defined for the gas.
The_Earth_System_Chapter_4.4: Figure 4-1 shows parallel solar beams falling on curved Earth. The same beam covers progressively more surface area toward the poles, so received solar energy per unit area decreases with latitude.
The_Earth_System_Chapter_4.5: Figure 4-2 compares absorbed solar energy and emitted infrared against latitude. Absorption exceeds emission in the tropics, while emission exceeds absorption at high latitudes; atmospheric and oceanic transport redistribute the surplus. Figure 4-3 shows paired Hadley cells: surface convergence and rising air at the ITCZ, poleward motion aloft, sinking near 30 degrees north/south, and surface return flow toward the equator.
The_Earth_System_Chapter_4.6: Figures 4-4 and 4-5 show the tropical cloud belt and deep convective towers. The bright ITCZ cloud band marks rising moist air, while clearer subtropical regions correspond to descending air. Condensation in the towers releases latent heat that helps drive the circulation.
The_Earth_System_Chapter_4.7: Figure 4-6 shows warm, less dense air rising over a wedge of cold polar air along the sloping polar front. Figure 4-7 combines tropical Hadley overturning with midlatitude/polar circulation, marking equatorial low pressure, subtropical highs, frontal regions, and polar highs.
The_Earth_System_Chapter_4.8: Figure 4-8 is a simplified globe showing north-south surface flow between pressure belts before rotational deflection is added. Figure 4-9 illustrates the Coriolis effect: Earth's eastward surface speed is greatest at the equator and declines poleward, so motion viewed from the rotating Earth appears deflected to the right in the Northern Hemisphere.
The_Earth_System_Chapter_4.9: Figure 4-10 resolves the outward centrifugal effect on east-west motion into vertical and horizontal components. Figure 4-11 adds Coriolis deflection to the global pressure belts, producing northeast/southeast trade winds, midlatitude westerlies, and polar easterlies, with convergence near the ITCZ.
The_Earth_System_Chapter_4.11: Box Figure 4-1 depicts a Northern Hemisphere hurricane as a low-pressure center with counterclockwise circulating winds. Pressure-gradient force points toward the low, while the Coriolis effect acts to the right of the motion; the surrounding text also discusses the inward acceleration associated with curved flow.
The_Earth_System_Chapter_4.12: Figure 4-12 compares warm tropical and cold polar air columns. The warmer column is deeper, pressure surfaces slope downward toward the pole, and the upper-level pressure gradient is strongest in the midlatitudes. Figure 4-13 shows geostrophic balance: pressure-gradient and Coriolis forces oppose one another, so wind flows parallel to the isobars rather than directly from high to low pressure.
The_Earth_System_Chapter_4.13: Figure 4-14 maps January 300-mbar height contours over the Northern Hemisphere; their wavy pattern depicts large upper-air waves. Figure 4-15 shows Earth's orbit at the two solstices and equinoxes with the axis retaining its tilt. Seasonal illumination is controlled by axial tilt; the hemisphere tilted toward the Sun has summer.
The_Earth_System_Chapter_4.14: Figure 4-16 compares June and December circulation. The ITCZ and associated circulation belts migrate toward the summer hemisphere; the winter hemisphere has a stronger equator-to-pole temperature contrast.
The_Earth_System_Chapter_4.15: Figure 4-17 contrasts daytime sea breeze and nighttime land breeze. Daytime heating gives lower surface pressure over land and onshore flow; nighttime land cooling can reverse the pressure difference and produce offshore flow, with return circulation aloft.
The_Earth_System_Chapter_4.16: Figure 4-18(a) maps January temperature contours. Northern continental interiors are much colder than nearby oceans at similar latitude, while the thermal equator lies mostly south of its July position. The map continues on the next PDF page.
The_Earth_System_Chapter_4.17: Figure 4-18(b,c) shows July temperatures and the annual temperature range. The thermal equator shifts north in July. Seasonal ranges are largest in northern continental interiors and small over tropical oceans, illustrating continentality and oceanic temperature moderation.
The_Earth_System_Chapter_4.18: Figure 4-19 compares mean sea-level pressure for January and July in millibars. Northern continents have strong winter highs and summer lows; oceanic subtropical highs and the ITCZ shift with season. The Southern Hemisphere pattern is more nearly zonal because oceans dominate its midlatitudes.
The_Earth_System_Chapter_4.19: Figure 4-20 maps satellite-derived Pacific surface winds using arrows for direction and shading for speed. It shows trade-wind convergence near the ITCZ and circulation around subtropical pressure systems, with smaller weather disturbances superimposed on the broad belts.
The_Earth_System_Chapter_4.20: Figure 4-21 compares Southeast Asian monsoon circulation. In June-July, heated land and low pressure draw moist air inland from the Indian Ocean, producing wet conditions. In December-January, high pressure over the cold continent drives dry outward flow and the main tropical rain belt shifts south. Figure 4-22's Earth image emphasizes the extensive ocean reservoir and cloud cover.
The_Earth_System_Chapter_4.21: Figure 4-23 connects solid ice, liquid water, and vapor. Melting, evaporation, and sublimation absorb energy; freezing, condensation, and deposition release energy. Opposite arrows pair the forward and reverse phase changes.
The_Earth_System_Chapter_4.22: Figure 4-24 shows the hydrologic cycle. Ocean/land evaporation supplies atmospheric water, winds advect it, and precipitation returns it to the surface; runoff, subsurface flow, and groundwater carry water back to the ocean. Its reservoir-and-flux diagram distinguishes the ocean's very large stored volume from the atmosphere's small store but rapid exchange, and balances net ocean evaporation with net land precipitation and runoff.
The_Earth_System_Chapter_4.23: Figure 4-25 plots saturation vapor pressure against temperature, rising steeply as temperature increases. An unsaturated point can reach the curve either by adding water vapor at fixed temperature or by cooling at fixed vapor pressure. This explains why uplift and cooling promote condensation.
The_Earth_System_Chapter_4.24: Figure 4-26 compares January and July precipitation maps. Rainfall belts migrate seasonally with the ITCZ, and summer monsoon rainfall is especially prominent over South and Southeast Asia. Subtropical desert regions remain comparatively dry.
The_Earth_System_Chapter_4.25: Figure 4-27 locates the world's major arid and semiarid regions and includes examples from the Sonoran, Taklimakan, Atacama, and Kalahari deserts. The geography illustrates several routes to dryness: subtropical subsidence, continental interiors, rain shadows, and cold-current west coasts.
